prospects.thesis: Leidos combines defense IT services with a growing digital modernization and AI-enabled national security franchise, trading at just 0.8x sales despite a strong federal budget tailwind. Bullish options and institutional flow alongside +7.7% one-month momentum suggest smart money is positioning ahead of continued DoD/civilian agency contract wins. Valuation offers a defensive entry into the defense-tech theme without paying a prime contractor premium.

Microsoft remains the purest large-cap AI monetization story via Azure OpenAI, Copilot attach rates across M365, and enterprise Fabric adoption, with +21.1% one-month momentum reflecting accelerating cloud growth. Bullish options and institutional signals confirm conviction into the next earnings cycle. Despite a 10.5x P/S, the durability of AI-driven cloud demand justifies inclusion as the anchor AI holding.

RTX offers diversified exposure across Raytheon missile systems, Pratt & Whitney engines, and Collins Aerospace, benefiting from replenishment demand (Patriot, SM-6) and a commercial aerospace aftermarket recovery. The GTF durability issues are largely priced in, and +10.9% one-month strength with bullish options/institutional flow signals a re-rating underway. Different sub-niche than LDOS (prime hardware vs. IT services) preserves diversification.

SMCI is the leading AI server/liquid-cooling integrator riding hyperscaler and sovereign AI capex, and at 0.5x sales with a -4.7% one-month pullback it offers the best risk/reward entry on the list. Bullish options positioning suggests traders are anticipating a rebound as accounting overhangs fade and Blackwell shipments ramp. This provides the semis/AI-infrastructure diversification missing from the other picks.

HII is the sole builder of U.S. nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and one of two Virginia-class submarine yards, giving it a structurally protected backlog amplified by AUKUS and Columbia-class demand. At 0.9x sales with +7.7% momentum and bullish institutional flow, it captures the naval/shipbuilding sub-niche distinct from LDOS (services) and RTX (missiles/aero). Multi-year submarine industrial base funding provides a durable catalyst.

market_pulse.rotation_analysis: Here's what's interesting: big money is piling into the classic "defensive yield + hard asset" trio — Utilities, Real Estate, and Energy — which usually happens when smart money expects interest rates to fall (helping REITs and utility dividends look more attractive) while also hedging against sticky inflation via energy. The Energy bid specifically lines up with the current administration's drill-baby-drill posture, LNG export permitting, and ongoing Middle East and Russia sanctions noise keeping a floor under crude. On the other side, they're aggressively hedging or dumping Industrials, Financials, Tech, and — most tellingly — Consumer Staples, where the put/call ratio is a jaw-dropping 12.6; that Staples signal is weird because Staples is *supposed* to be defensive, so someone is betting that even Walmart-and-Procter-type names get hit, likely from tariff pass-through costs squeezing margins and GLP-1 drugs continuing to eat into packaged food volumes. Industrials getting hammered despite all the infrastructure and reshoring headlines tells me the options market thinks the tariff regime is going to hurt multinationals more than the "Made in America" narrative helps them, and widening credit spreads plus bearish HYG/LQD flow confirms bond desks smell trouble — historically this combo precedes a 5-10% equity wobble within 4-8 weeks. The contradiction worth noting: Tech stocks have been ripping, but a 2.57 put/call ratio means institutions are quietly buying crash insurance behind the scenes, which usually means they're riding the momentum but don't trust it. The non-obvious inference the headlines are missing: this isn't a "recession trade" or a "growth trade" — it's a *stagflation-lite* positioning, where money is fleeing anything exposed
